title: The cultural niche: Why social learning is essential for human adaptation
central_proposition: Human adaptation and success across diverse habitats are primarily due to a uniquely developed capacity for cumulative cultural learning, which allows for the intergenerational accumulation of complex, locally adaptive knowledge and practices beyond individual inventive capacities.

concept_definitions.name: cognitive niche
concept_definitions.definition: a suite of uniquely flexible cognitive capacities that allow our species to acquire locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments.

concept_definitions.name: cultural niche
concept_definitions.definition: our uniquely developed ability to learn from others... This capacity enables humans to gradually accumulate information across generations and develop well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices that no individual could invent on their own.

concept_definitions.name: dedicated intelligence
concept_definitions.definition: domain-specific learning and decision-making mechanisms that are adapted to particular environments.

concept_definitions.name: improvisational intelligence
concept_definitions.definition: a suite of uniquely flexible cognitive capacities that allow our species to acquire locally adaptive behavior in a wide range of environments.

concept_definitions.name: cumulative cultural evolution
concept_definitions.definition: social learning allows the gradual cumulative cultural evolution of complex, locally adaptive behaviors that individuals could not learn on their own.

argument_structure: The paper critiques the dominant 'cognitive niche' hypothesis, which attributes human adaptability to superior individual cognitive abilities, by presenting ethnographic and historical evidence demonstrating its insufficiency. It then proposes the 'cultural niche' hypothesis, arguing that cumulative cultural learning, driven by an evolved social learning psychology, is the primary mechanism for human adaptation. It details the coevolutionary logic of how social learning increases population fitness and leads to complex adaptations, even without individual causal understanding, and discusses how this cultural niche has shaped human biology and can lead to maladaptation.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: Human adaptation relies on cumulative cultural evolution, enabled by an evolved social learning psychology. Individual learning is often too costly or difficult for complex environments. Social learning, while cheaper, only leads to adaptation if it increases the population's ability to *create* adaptive information, not just spread it. This occurs through selective learning strategies: individuals learn individually when environmental cues are clear/cheap, and culturally when cues are costly/inaccurate. This evolved psychology includes an 'information quality threshold' that arbitrates between individual and cultural learning. Additionally, cultural learning allows for the accumulation of small, intergenerational improvements and the spread of successful traits through prestige-biased copying, even without causal understanding. This cultural niche, in turn, creates new selection pressures on human biology (e.g., brain size, specialized cognitive abilities) in a gene-culture coevolutionary loop. However, the same social learning biases can also lead to the spread of maladaptive beliefs or practices.

findings.antecedent: Individual human cognitive ability (e.g., improvisational intelligence, bigger brains, computing power)
findings.consequent: Ability to adapt to a wide range of environments
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to 'figure out how to live in a wide range of environments' by 'cause-and-effect reasoning to make inferences about local environmental contingencies.'
findings.quote: Humans have relatively bigger brains and more computing power, and this allows us to adapt to a wider range of environments than other animals.

findings.antecedent: Individual human cognitive abilities (e.g., improvisational intelligence)
findings.consequent: Sufficient for acquiring all information necessary to survive in any single habitat
findings.mechanism: The paper argues that even in simple societies, the required knowledge (tools, local knowledge, social arrangements) is too vast and complex for any single individual to invent or understand fully.
findings.quote: none of us is nearly smart enough to acquire all of the information necessary to survive in any single habitat.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ethnographic accounts of Inuit, lost European explorer experiments, loss of technology in isolated populations.

findings.antecedent: Uniquely developed ability to learn from others (social learning, culture)
findings.consequent: Human adaptation and success across diverse habitats
findings.mechanism: Enables gradual accumulation of information across generations, leading to well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices too complex for individual invention.
findings.quote: We owe our success to our uniquely developed ability to learn from others.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Ethnographic accounts of Inuit, lost European explorer experiments (Amundsen vs. Franklin), loss/reintroduction of technology in isolated populations (Tasmanian, Polar Inuit).

findings.consequent: Human ability to inhabit a diverse range of environments
findings.mechanism: The paper argues that cultural adaptations are the primary driver, not genetic ones, for rapid global expansion.
findings.quote: local genetic changes have played only a relatively small part in our ability to inhabit such a diverse range of environments
findings.empirical_support_cited: Much evidence indicates, in fact, that local genetic changes have played only a relatively small part in our ability to inhabit such a diverse range of environments (9, 10).

findings.consequent: Cost of acquiring locally adaptive information
findings.mechanism: Allows individuals to acquire information from others, avoiding the costs of individual trial-and-error learning.
findings.quote: This capacity that dramatically lowers the cost of acquiring information necessary for local, contingent adaptations.

findings.antecedent: Social learning as mere 'free riding' (copying without contributing to innovation)
findings.consequent: Population's ability to adapt to varying environments / average fitness
findings.mechanism: Imitators spread until they erode the benefits of free riding, as the proportion of innovators decreases, leading to no net gain in adaptive information for the population.
findings.quote: if this is the only benefit of social learning, there will be no increase in the ability of the population to adapt
findings.empirical_support_cited: evolutionary models show that if this is the only benefit of social learning, there will be no increase in the ability of the population to adapt (31–34).

findings.antecedent: Evolved social learning psychology (with adaptive biases)
findings.consequent: Population's ability to create adaptive information / average fitness
findings.mechanism: Social learning must increase the population's ability to *create* adaptive information, not just spread it. This happens through selective learning strategies.
findings.quote: cultural learning can increase average fitness only if it increases the ability of the population to create adaptive information (32).
findings.empirical_support_cited: models assume that our learning psychology has a genetically heritable 'information quality threshold' that governs whether an individual relies on inferences from environmental cues or learns from others.

findings.antecedent: Opportunities to learn from experience or by observation of the world (environmental cues)
findings.consequent: Advantage of selective learning (individual vs. social)
findings.mechanism: When environmental cues are clear and cheap, individual learning is favored. When cues are costly or inaccurate, cultural learning is favored. An evolved psychology arbitrates this.
findings.quote: The ability to learn or imitate selectively is advantageous because opportunities to learn from experience or by observation of the world vary.

findings.antecedent: Low information quality threshold (in learning psychology)
findings.consequent: Reliance on individual learning (from environmental cues)
findings.mechanism: Individuals with a low threshold rely on even poor cues to learn individually, as they are more likely to make accurate or low-cost inferences.
findings.quote: Individuals with a low information quality threshold rely on even poor cues, whereas individuals with a high threshold usually imitate.

findings.antecedent: High information quality threshold (in learning psychology)
findings.mechanism: Individuals with a high threshold require strong environmental cues to learn individually; otherwise, they imitate, as this is the more adaptive strategy when individual learning is difficult.
findings.quote: Individuals with a low information quality threshold rely on even poor cues, whereas individuals with a high threshold usually imitate.

findings.antecedent: Difficulty of individual learning (e.g., complex problems, costly/inaccurate environmental cues)
findings.mechanism: When individual learning is difficult, the evolved psychology favors imitation, even if environmental cues suggest alternative behaviors, leading to cumulative cultural adaptation.
findings.quote: often only a minority will be able to solve the adaptive problem on the basis of environmental cues alone, because the appropriate environmental cues are rare or the adaptive problem is too complex.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Inuit adaptations (implied by the complexity of their tools/practices).

findings.consequent: Accumulation of acquired improvements across generations
findings.mechanism: Cultural learners start their search for optimal designs closer to the best existing design (from previous generations' improvements) and can invest in further improvements, which are then transmitted.
findings.quote: The ability to learn culturally can also raise the average fitness of a population by allowing acquired improvements to accumulate from one generation to the next.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Historical accounts of technology (37, 38), evolution of kayak keels (41).

findings.antecedent: Learners comparing success of individuals modeling different behaviors
findings.consequent: Spread of traits correlated with success (even without causal understanding)
findings.mechanism: Imitators copy successful individuals, assuming their traits contribute to success. This allows adaptive traits to spread, even if the imitator doesn't understand the causal link or copies irrelevant traits.
findings.quote: a propensity to imitate the successful can lead to the spread of traits that are correlated with success, even though imitators have no causal understanding of the connection.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Laboratory and field evidence (42), developmental psychology (43, 44, 45).

findings.antecedent: Children observing adult models perform actions (necessary and unnecessary)
findings.mechanism: Children implicitly assume that if the model performed an action, it was probably important, even if they don't understand why.
findings.quote: Children accurately copy all steps, including steps that direct visual inspection would suggest are unnecessary.

findings.antecedent: Human food preferences (e.g., for chili peppers)
findings.mechanism: Heavily influenced by preferences of others (social learning), leading to reinterpretation of pain as pleasure/excitement.
findings.quote: observational learning leads people to reinterpret their pain as pleasure or excitement

findings.consequent: Adaptive outcomes (e.g., reduced fish poisoning during pregnancy/lactation)
findings.mechanism: Taboos are learned and transmitted, sustained by selective learning from prestigious women, even if individuals offer different causal explanations or lack understanding of the adaptive reason.
findings.quote: Food taboos targeting these species during pregnancy and lactation prohibit women from eating these species and reduce the incidence of fish poisoning during this period.

findings.antecedent: Cognitive or social processes making maladaptive ideas common (e.g., weak cognitive biases, prestige bias)
findings.consequent: Spread of maladaptive beliefs and practices
findings.mechanism: The same propensity to acquire common behavior (from cultural learning) can lead to maladaptation if the ideas are not patently false or harmful, especially if associated with prestige.
findings.quote: if there are cognitive or social processes that make maladaptive ideas common, and these ideas are not patently false or harmful, people will adopt these ideas as well.
findings.empirical_support_cited: Laboratory diffusion chain studies (59), Boyer (60) on supernatural beliefs, Henrich (61) on costly displays.

findings.antecedent: Cultural niche (human reliance on cumulative cultural learning)
findings.consequent: New selection pressures on human biology (e.g., bigger brains, specialized cognitive abilities)
findings.mechanism: The availability of large amounts of valuable cultural information favored the evolution of biological traits that enhance its acquisition, storage, organization, and retrieval.
findings.quote: The availability of large amounts of valuable cultural information would have favored the evolution of bigger brains equipped to acquire, store, organize, and retrieve cultural information
findings.empirical_support_cited: Rapid increase in human encephalization over the last 500,000 y, evolution of specialized cognitive abilities (theory of mind, social referencing, overimitation, functional understanding of artifacts, taxonomic inheritance) (62, 45, 52, 63).

findings.antecedent: Culturally evolved techniques and products (e.g., fire, cooking, weapons, tools)
findings.consequent: New selection pressures acting on human bones, muscles, teeth, and guts
findings.mechanism: Cultural innovations alter the environment and behaviors, which in turn drives biological evolution.
findings.quote: The presence of culturally evolved techniques and products such as fire, cooking, weapons, and tools created new selection pressures acting on our bones, muscles, teeth, and guts (9).

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: Populations in environments where individual learning is difficult or costly will exhibit a stronger reliance on cultural learning (imitation) compared to populations in environments where individual learning is easier.
The complexity of adaptive technologies in a population will correlate with the population's history of cumulative cultural learning, rather than solely with individual cognitive capacity.

Experimental studies will show that individuals, especially children, will overimitate actions, even seemingly irrelevant ones, when learning from a model, particularly if the model is perceived as successful or prestigious.
The spread of maladaptive beliefs or practices can be predicted by the presence of weak cognitive biases or social learning biases (e.g., prestige bias) in experimental diffusion chains.

Genetic evidence will show coevolutionary signatures between genes related to cognitive capacities (e.g., brain size, social learning) and the historical trajectory of cultural complexity in human lineages.
bridge_warrants: The paper explicitly contrasts its 'cultural niche' with the 'cognitive niche' hypothesis (Tooby, Cosmides, Pinker), arguing that the latter overestimates individual intelligence and underestimates culture.
It connects to evolutionary models of social learning (Rogers, Boyd & Richerson, Lehmann, Rendell et al.).
It links to developmental psychology research on imitation and social learning (Lyons, Nielsen, Whiten, Birch).
It connects to historical accounts of technology evolution (Basalla, Petroski, Johnson).
It touches on gene-culture coevolution (Richerson & Boyd).
methodological_critiques: The paper critiques the 'cognitive niche' hypothesis for 'overestimat[ing] the extent to which individual human cognitive abilities allow people to succeed in diverse environments and misunderstand[ing] the role that culture plays in a number of important ways.'
It critiques models of social learning that only consider it as a cost-saving mechanism, arguing they fail to show how it increases population adaptation.
model_structure: The paper proposes a coevolutionary model where environmental challenges drive selection for social learning strategies. These evolved psychologies enable cumulative cultural evolution, allowing humans to adapt to diverse environments beyond individual cognitive capacity. This cultural niche, in turn, creates new selection pressures on human biology (e.g., brain size, specific cognitive modules), leading to gene-culture coevolution. The model also accounts for maladaptation arising from the same social learning biases.

paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: In the last 60,000 y humans have expanded across the globe and now occupy a wider range than any other terrestrial species. Our ability to successfully adapt to such a diverse range of habitats is often explained in terms of our cognitive ability. Humans have relatively bigger brains and more computing power than other animals, and this allows us to figure out how to live in a wide range of environments. Here we argue that humans may be smarter than other creatures, but none of us is nearly smart enough to acquire all of the information necessary to survive in any single habitat. In even the simplest foraging societies, people depend on a vast array of tools, detailed bodies of local knowledge, and complex social arrangements and often do not understand why these tools, beliefs, and behaviors are adaptive. We owe our success to our uniquely developed ability to learn from others. This capacity enables humans to gradually accumulate information across generations and develop well-adapted tools, beliefs, and practices that are too complex for any single individual to invent during their lifetime.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Social learning and cumulative culture create a cultural niche that is essential for human adaptation to diverse environments.

mechanism_chain.description: The paper argues that social learning facilitates the accumulation of cultural knowledge and practices, which in turn leads to the construction of a cultural niche that enables human adaptation to a wide range of environments.

steps.to_construct: Accumulation of cultural knowledge and practices (cumulative culture)
